name: Basílica del Voto Nacional
label: Basílica del Voto
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'El Panecillo' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Salon del Reino Testigos de Jehová Panecillo' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q4868435: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Neo-Gothic basilica with gargoyles shaped like local animals.

text.description: The Basílica del Voto Nacional is a Roman Catholic church in the historic centre of Quito, and it reaches up to 83 m in height. Its twin towers and pale front stand out above the colonial rooftops. That makes it easy to photograph from a distance, with the whole building set against the city. The idea came from Father Julio Matovelle in 1883, as a lasting reminder of Ecuador's consecration to the Sacred Heart. The architect Emilio Tarlier took his inspiration from Bourges Cathedral. The first stone was laid in 1892, and the basilica was consecrated in 1988. It is still described as unfinished, and a local legend says the world will end when it is completed. The best-known angle is from El Panecillo, the hill to the south. From there the towers and south façade rise over the rooftops, with the hill's Virgin statue in the foreground. Guides often call it the standard postcard view. Two closer alternatives are Venezuela y Carchi, for a low upward view of both towers against the sky, and Calle Venezuela, where the church fills the view along the street. The basilica also holds the National Pantheon of Ecuador in its crypt. Visitors can climb to a viewing platform for a fee, but that gives a view of the city, not of the church itself.
text.geographic_location: The basilica stands in Quito's historic centre. El Panecillo, the hill just south of the old town, is the recommended viewpoint for looking across the rooftops towards it.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops listed for this spot. For the classic view, head towards El Panecillo. For the closer street views, head towards Calle Venezuela in the historic centre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer. Use the default lens (1x) when you want the Virgin statue and the whole skyline in the shot. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the street, where you are close to the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in El Panecillo (hill to the south, looking north across the historic centre). The basilica's twin towers and south façade rise above the colonial rooftops, with the hill's Virgin statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the towers on one of the vertical lines, with the rooftops filling the lower third. Include a corner of the Virgin statue for depth. For an alternative, go down to Venezuela y Carchi, hold the phone low and tilt it up to fit both towers against the sky, or walk along Calle Venezuela to fill the frame with the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and detail. Hold the phone steady against a wall or railing if you can. After dark, try night mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, or after dark when the building is lit, according to one guide.

text.access_note: El Panecillo is a public park, but the church is a place of worship and the tower climb is ticketed, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.

name: TelefériQo
label: TelefériQo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cruz Loma' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cruz Loma' (node/346124997): point.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Cable car up the slope of Pichincha volcano.

text.description: The TelefériQo is a gondola lift that climbs the east side of Pichincha Volcano from the edge of Quito's city centre to the Cruz Loma lookout. It opened in July 2005 and is one of the highest aerial lifts in the world, rising from 3,117 m to 3,945 m. The ride takes about twenty minutes. That height is why it photographs so well: from the top, the city is spread out along the valley below, with the Andean volcanoes behind it when the sky is clear. The cabins can also be seen heading down the mountain towards the city. The best frame is from the main railing at the Cruz Loma lookout beside the upper station. Guides often single out this railing for wide city views, and from the top station you can also include the cable car in your shot. Itchimbia Park is a free alternative, but the cable car's line looks small from there. It is cooler and windier up top than in the city, and fog can drift in, especially in the morning. Some people feel the altitude, so go slowly and give yourself time to settle in before you start shooting. There is a public restroom, a small cafe and a few shops at the top. Check the weather before you commit to the ride.
text.geographic_location: On the east side of Pichincha Volcano, above the edge of Quito's city centre. The lower station is at the edge of the centre and the Cruz Loma lookout is at the top of the line.
text.directions_text: Head for the lower station of the TelefériQo at the edge of Quito's city centre. Ride the gondola for about twenty minutes up to the Cruz Loma lookout. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view over the city. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the volcanoes and sky, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the gondola cabins on the slope.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (main railing at the Cruz Loma lookout beside the upper station). Wide view over the city spread across the valley, with the Andean volcanoes behind and the gondola cabins descending against the mountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line so the city gets most of the frame. Use the railing or the edge of the upper station as a foreground. If you want the cable car in the picture, zoom in on a cabin and let the city blur behind it. For a more distant, free-of-charge alternative, Itchimbia Park shows the line on the western slopes, but it looks small there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the volcanoes to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the clouds keep their detail. Try panorama for the full sweep of the valley, and hold the phone steady against the railing if it is windy. Live Photos can capture the moving cabins.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekday mornings, roughly 9:00 to 11:00, when the sky is usually clearest and it is least crowded. Fog can still form in the morning, so check the weather first, because afternoon cloud often hides the volcanoes.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed ride, and a photo ID is needed to buy a lift ticket and the stub must be kept for the return, so check the official site for current prices and opening hours before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the Cruz Loma lookout the lift line runs downhill to the east, towards the city.
Holding the phone steady against the railing helps keep shots sharp in wind.

name: Virgin of El Panecillo
label: Virgin of El Panecillo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mirador del Panecillo' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Mirador Panecillo' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/302694122: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'La Virgen de El Panecillo' (13 m across).
notes: Winged Virgin statue on a hill with views over the old town.

text.description:
The Virgin of El Panecillo stands on top of a loaf-shaped hill beside Quito's historic centre, and she can be seen from much of the city. At 41 metres including the base, it is the tallest statue in Ecuador and the tallest aluminium statue in the world. It is a large version of the Virgin of Quito, a small wooden sculpture carved by Bernardo de Legarda in 1734. The Spanish sculptor Agustín de la Herrán Matorras designed it. It was built from 7,400 numbered aluminium pieces, shipped over and put together on the hilltop, and finished on 28 March 1975.

For photographs there are two good subjects in one place: the winged statue itself, and the view from beside her. The Mirador del Panecillo, a platform inside the base reached by stairs, gives wide panoramic views of the old town and the volcanoes behind it (check on the day how wide the view is). You can also stay outside, look up, and fill the frame with the Virgin against the sky, with the city spread out behind her. If you want to see the whole hill with the statue in the skyline, Vista Hermosa is another viewpoint to try, though check its exact location before you set out.

The statue is huge and you will be close to her, so expect to switch between a wide shot for the scene and a tighter one for her face and wings. Allow a little time at the railings for the city views, especially if the light is changing.
text.geographic_location: On top of El Panecillo, the loaf-shaped hill that rises just beside Quito's historic centre and looks over the old town.
text.directions_text: Start from the historic centre of Quito and head towards the hill of El Panecillo, which rises beside the historic centre and is easy to spot because the statue stands on top. Several guides advise going up by taxi rather than walking the approach, so we suggest a taxi. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens to fit the statue and her base into one frame when you are close. Use the default lens (1x) for the city views. Try the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as her face, her wings or the volcanoes in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (viewing platform inside the base of the statue, reached by the stairs in the monument). The statue seen from close range with a 360-degree panorama of the historic centre and the surrounding volcanoes behind it. The statue is to the north-west of you, so you can see her whole figure with room to step back and choose your framing. It offers wide panoramic views of the historic centre and the surrounding volcanoes, and the fee is small but may have changed, so be ready to check on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a line so the city does not lean. From where you stand, use the default lens (1x) for the statue and the old town, and keep a church tower or the volcanoes on a third of the frame. Closer in, at the foot of the monument, tilt the phone up with the ultra-wide (0.5x) and let the wings fill the frame with sky behind. For the panorama mode, move slowly and keep the phone upright. As an alternative, Virgen del Panecillo gives the aluminium Virgin filling the frame from below with the city behind her, and Vista Hermosa shows the hill and statue in the skyline above the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the city to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the statue does not turn white. When the lights come on in the evening, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and blue hour, when the city lights come on, are the most recommended. Some guides prefer early morning to avoid crowds, so choose what suits your day.

text.access_note: The hilltop is a public viewpoint, but the platform inside the base of the statue is paid. The fee is reported to be small but may have changed, so check before you go.

name: Plaza de la Independencia
label: Independence Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Independencia' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W24734054 (Plaza de la Independencia): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Main square of the old town with the Independence Monument.

text.description: Plaza de la Independencia is a broad open square in Quito, and its main appeal for photographs is the way the buildings around it frame the space. The cathedral, the Carondelet Presidential Palace, the Archbishop's Palace and the Municipal Palace all face onto the plaza, so one wide frame can take in all four. It is a good place to practise composing a scene rather than a single monument. For the full-square panorama, go to the phone icon on the map in the northwest part of the square and look southeast. This angle shows the plaza with its surrounding palaces. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens to fit the whole scene, and keep the phone level with the gridlines turned on so the building edges stay straight. Then try the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of one side, or zoom in for details of the façades. For a second picture, walk to the southern side of the square and photograph the Archbishop's Palace with the open space and benches in the foreground. Guides say the square looks best in soft early-morning light, before the crowds and street vendors fill it, so an early visit gives you cleaner, emptier frames. The square itself is a free, open public space. Entry to the surrounding buildings is not covered here.
text.geographic_location: Plaza de la Independencia is a square in Quito, surrounded by the cathedral and the Carondelet Presidential Palace, with the Archbishop's Palace and the Municipal Palace also facing onto it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local map or transport app for the best way to reach it. Navigate to Plaza de la Independencia in Quito. Once in the square, head to the phone icon on the map in the northwest part of the square and turn to look southeast. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full-square view. Use the default lens (1x) for one side of the plaza at a time. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details of the palace façades.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see a wide view of the square, with the cathedral, the Carondelet Presidential Palace, the Archbishop's Palace and the Municipal Palace framing the plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. Leave some open square in the foreground to give a sense of space. For a different view, walk to the southern edge and frame the Archbishop's Palace with the open space and benches in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Try panorama mode for the sweep of the whole square, moving slowly and steadily. Tap on a building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds and street vendors fill the square, when guides say the light is soft.

text.access_note: The square is a free, open public space. Entry to the cathedral or the surrounding palaces is not covered here.

name: Quito Metropolitan Cathedral
label: Metropolitan Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Independencia' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de la Independencia' (way/24734054): middle (166 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Quito Metropolitan Cathedral'.

text.description:
Quito's cathedral is a long white-painted church on the southwest side of the Plaza de la Independencia, also called the Plaza Grande. It has served as a cathedral since the 1540s, and in 1995 it became the Cathedral of Ecuador, the senior Catholic church in the country. It was consecrated in 1572 and has been repaired after several earthquakes and a volcanic eruption, so what you see is the result of many rebuildings.

A surprise for first-time visitors is that the building turns its long side to the square. A deep ravine at the time of construction stopped the main front from facing the plaza. The grand entrance with the belltower looks onto Calle García Moreno instead. What faces the plaza is the arched side doorway, known as the Carondelet Arch, with its curved staircase and a long stone parapet decorated with spheres and pyramids.

That makes it a good subject for a phone. The white wall, the arch and the parapet give you clear lines and a strong sense of scale, and the open square lets you step back far enough to fit a lot in. Look for the green domes and the belltower rising above the roofline. For a very different picture, the rooftop and dome climb gives views over the old town, and El Panecillo gives a distant view of the whole historic centre.
text.geographic_location: In Quito's historic centre, on the southwest side of the Plaza de la Independencia (Plaza Grande), with its long side facing the square and its belltower end on Calle García Moreno.
text.directions_text: No Quito transport stops are listed for this spot, so start from the historic centre and the Plaza de la Independencia. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole side of the cathedral across the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the parapet and arch in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Carondelet Arch, the belltower and the domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la Independencia (northeast part of the square, facing the cathedral's main facade and its arched entrance). The white cathedral front with its bell tower and green domes, framed by the open plaza and the Plaza Grande's central monument. The belltower stands at one end of the building and the domes rise behind the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the stone parapet along the lower third so the building does not look tilted. Keep the arch slightly off-centre and include some open plaza in the foreground for scale. For a second view, try the paid rooftop climb or the distant outlook from El Panecillo, which shows the green domes among the old-town rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the white paint keeps its detail against the sky. Take a few shots, because people crossing the square may walk through your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white walls than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public square. The cathedral is an active place of worship, interior photography is generally not allowed, and the rooftop and dome climb is paid, so check the official site before you go.

name: La Carolina Park
label: La Carolina Park
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31133611: large area 'Parque La Carolina' (1719 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large city park in the modern centre.

text.description: La Carolina Park is a big, open green space in Quito's central business district, surrounded by the busy city around it. That mix is why it photographs well: you can frame grass, trees and people in the foreground and let the city beyond the park sit behind them. The park covers about 165 acres (670,000 square metres) and is bordered by Avenida Río Amazonas, Avenida de los Shyris, Avenida Naciones Unidas, Avenida Eloy Alfaro and Avenida de la República. It grew from a farm that was taken over in 1939. In 1985 Pope John Paul II led a large open-air Catholic mass here, and a giant Christian cross was built to mark the place. Quiteños come mostly at weekends to play football, basketball and ecua-volley, and to run, fly kites, snack or simply watch the world go by. Artists sometimes perform too. That makes it a good place for relaxed, candid scenes. The park is so large that you should pick one view rather than try to capture it all. Look for a path leading away from you, a group of players, or kites against the sky, and keep a few people in the frame to give a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: La Carolina Park sits in the centre of Quito's central business district, between Avenida Río Amazonas, Avenida de los Shyris, Avenida Naciones Unidas, Avenida Eloy Alfaro and Avenida de la República. The Quito Exhibition Center, the botanical gardens and a vivarium are in its western part.
text.directions_text: Paths inside the park are open and easy to follow. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the open lawns and the sense of space. Use the default lens (1x) for most scenes with people and paths. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out kites, players or distant details without walking over to them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (at the start of the perimeter loop, after the parking lot). The large monumental cross in the foreground with the park's green edge and, from the loop, a view toward the financial district towers. From there, face north towards the subject inside the park and take in the open ground ahead of you, rather than turning around in all directions.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper third line so the grass and sky both get room. Use a path or a row of trees as a leading line, and include a few people for scale. For a view that includes the surroundings, use the default lens (1x) with trees framing one side, and try the ultra-wide (0.5x) held low for a bigger sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a Live Photo when kites or games are in motion, so you can pick the best frame afterwards. For a wide scene, panorama mode works well on the open lawns if you hold the phone steady and sweep slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekends are livelier, with games and kite flying, so they suit photos with people in them. For softer light and fewer shadows, go in the morning or late afternoon.

text.access_note: This is a large public park, but check the official site before you go for any events, closures or rules covering the exhibition centre, botanical gardens and vivarium in its western part.

name: La Capilla del Hombre
label: Capilla del Hombre
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31152844: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo Capilla del Hombre' (56 m across).
notes: Museum of Oswaldo Guayasamín's art with city views.

text.description:
La Capilla del Hombre ("The Chapel of Man") is an art museum in the Bellavista area, high enough to look out over Quito. It was designed by the painter Oswaldo Guayasamín together with Handel Guayasamín, and it is dedicated to the peoples of Latin America. Building work began in 1995 and was finished in 2002, after the painter's death. Inside, his paintings, sculptures and murals tell the story of suffering and violence in Latin America and the wider world, and the building itself is meant to work with its surroundings as part of that message.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the strong, simple shapes of the building set against the city and sky beyond. Start with a wide view that shows the whole structure and its setting, then move closer for details such as edges, textures and the lines where the walls meet the sky. People standing near the walls give a useful sense of scale. Keep the phone level, since a tilted horizon or leaning walls are easy to spot in architectural pictures. Switch on gridlines to help. If the day is bright, tap on a mid-tone part of the wall and lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps some colour. Photography rules inside the museum can differ from the outside, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: On a site in Bellavista overlooking the city, close to the Guayasamín foundation and museum.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed close to the spot, so start from the Bellavista area of Quito and come by taxi or hired scooter. Ask the driver for La Capilla del Hombre, and check the official site for the current entrance details before you travel. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole building and its setting, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. A telephoto/zoom lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) helps isolate details of the walls and shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the edges of the building up with them to keep verticals straight. Include a patch of sky above and, if the view allows, a hint of the city to show the setting overlooking it. Then take a few close-ups of textures and sculptural details with the default lens (1x) or a little zoom.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the building, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Portrait mode is better kept for photos of people, not for the architecture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the walls of the building and gives the sky more colour than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: It is a museum, so access is likely to be ticketed with set visiting times; check the official site before you go.

name: Basilica and Convent of San Francisco, Quito
label: San Francisco Convent
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de San Francisco' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de San Francisco' (way/376087703): middle (163 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/159408371: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iglesia de San Francisco' (111 m across).
notes: Oldest colonial church complex in Quito.

text.description:
The Basilica and Convent of San Francisco is the big stone church and monastery facing the Plaza de San Francisco, in the middle of Quito's old town. It is described as the oldest and most significant religious site in Ecuador. It is also the largest architectural complex in any historic centre in South America, covering about three and a half hectares. Building work on the first church began around 1537, only a few years after the city was founded. Work on the current building started in 1550 and was finished around 1680, and it was officially inaugurated in 1705. Its Mannerist-Baroque facade sits above a curving flight of steps that links the church to the square, and the whole complex is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "City of Quito".

It photographs well because the square is open and large enough to fit the entire facade in one frame. The cobbled plaza in the foreground leads the eye towards the carved stonework and the towers. Stand at the far eastern edge of the square and take in the whole front, then move closer for details of the stone. Early morning light falls on the carving and the square is emptier, so you can keep people out of your composition more easily. Photography is generally not allowed inside the church, so plan to take all your pictures from outside.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Quito, facing the Plaza de San Francisco, near the corner of Av. José de Sucre and Sebastián de Benalcázar.
text.directions_text: Head for the Plaza de San Francisco in Quito's old town. From there it is about 1 minute on foot to reach the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and the open square in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved stonework and the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de San Francisco (far eastern edge, about 30–40 m back from the church entrance). The full stone facade of the church and monastery, with the open plaza in the foreground leading the eye toward it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone level so the facade does not lean. Leave some cobbles in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a different view, try Calle Cuenca, where the bell towers are framed by the colonial buildings along the cobbled street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky and pale stone keep their detail. If the plaza is busy, take a short burst of shots and pick the one with the fewest people in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise to about 8am gives the cleanest compositions, with the square emptier and early light on the carved stone. Late afternoon is also suggested for golden light.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the church is an active place of worship and the convent's bell tower and museum are a separate visit, so check the official site before you go.

sources.title: Basilica and Convent of San Francisco, Quito

name: La Ronda Street
label: Calle La Ronda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Juan de Dios Morales' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Juan de Dios Morales nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W31153096 (La Ronda Street): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Narrow colonial street with balconies and cafés.

text.description:
La Ronda Street is a narrow cobbled lane in Quito, known locally by that name. Its official name on the map is Calle Juan de Dios Morales. It photographs well because everything a phone likes is in one place: rows of colourful colonial-style facades, balconies, lanterns and cobbles, all leading the eye down a long, narrow view.

In late afternoon the low, warm sun falls on the painted walls and brings out their colours.

Start with the default lens (1x) and use the gridlines to keep the vertical walls straight. Let the cobbles run into the lower corner of the frame so the lane leads the eye. Then try the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the balconies, or 2x to squeeze the lantern-lined houses together. A second option is the lane's entrance, framed from the corner. If you want the street without other visitors in the shot, an emptier moment is worth waiting for.
text.geographic_location: La Ronda Street is a lane in central Quito.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or station stops listed for this spot, so go by taxi or on foot to Calle Juan de Dios Morales, known as La Ronda, in central Quito. It is about 768 m south-east of the street's mapped position, so the street is to the north-west of where you stand. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facades and balconies. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole lane and the sky above it. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to stack the lanterns and houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Juan de Dios Morales (western end, looking back along the lane). The colorful colonial facades, balconies and cobbles of the lane, lit by low warm sun coming in from the west. The view takes in the painted colonial facades, the balconies and the cobbles, with the low warm sun on them in late afternoon.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the house walls upright so they don't lean. Let the cobbles lead the eye into the frame and place the lanterns along one side. For a different view, try the lane's entrance from the corner, with the narrow street and the painted houses receding ahead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a sunlit wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright paint keeps its colour. If people walk through the frame, take a Live Photo and pick the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening, when the low warm sun lights the painted walls.

text.access_note: This is a public street with no entry charge listed, but shops, restaurants and other venues along it may have their own rules, so check local signs for any rules.

name: Church of La Compañía, Quito
label: La Compañía Church
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/673869411: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of the Society of Jesus' (96 m across).

text.description:
La Compañía is the Jesuit church in Quito's Historic Center, standing on the corner of García Moreno and Sucre streets. Its façade is carved entirely from grey volcanic stone, and that is what you will photograph first. Close up, the stonework is packed with detail, including carved plants and symbols of the Indigenous peoples of Ecuador. Inside, the walls and ceilings are covered in gold leaf, which has earned it nicknames such as the "Temple of Solomon of South America".

The Jesuits reached Quito in 1586, and the church took roughly 160 years to build under a succession of architects. The stone façade was finally finished on 24 July 1765. Baroque style dominates, though the building mixes four styles. Two popes have visited: John Paul II in 1985 and Francis in 2015.

For a phone, the church gives you two different kinds of picture. The first is the whole façade, which is tall and narrow beside the street. The second is a close-up of the carving, where the texture of the stone shows well. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, and leave a little space around the doorway rather than cutting it tight. If you go inside, photography rules may apply, so check the official site before you go and be respectful of people who are praying.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Center of Quito, on the corner of García Moreno and Sucre streets, a short way south of the Cathedral and Plaza Grande, on the same block as the Centro Cultural Metropolitano.
text.directions_text: Start from Plaza Grande and the Cathedral in the Historic Center, then head south along García Moreno towards the corner with Sucre, where the church stands. If you are coming from elsewhere in Quito, make your way to Plaza Grande and walk the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tall façade in from close range, and the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the doorway. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved stone details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the whole façade, step back from the doorway to the opposite side of the street if the pavement allows, and keep the front of the church in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the façade with the vertical lines so the stonework doesn't lean. Tilting the phone upwards will make the building lean, so hold it straight and step back instead. For a detail shot, use the telephoto on one carved section of the doorway and let the stone fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone on the screen to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the carving keeps its detail. If you take photos inside where it is allowed, use night mode for steadier results in low light, and hold the phone against a wall or pillar.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in front of the façade. Check the official site for visiting times.

text.access_note: A working church and popular visitor attraction, so dress respectfully and check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The church stands a short walk south of Plaza Grande and the Cathedral.
Stepping back to the opposite side of the street gives a fuller view of the façade, space and pavement permitting.
Photography rules may apply inside the church.
Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
Visitors should dress respectfully in a church.

name: Plaza de San Francisco, Quito
label: San Francisco Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Iglesia y Monasterio de San Francisco' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Iglesia y Convento de San Francisco' (pois); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q14054866: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Large cobbled square in front of the convent.

text.description: Plaza de San Francisco is a major public square in the Historic Centre of Quito, named after the Church and Convent of St. Francis that fronts it. The whitewashed church and monastery facade fills one side. Other buildings around the square include the Chapel of Villacís, the Chapel of Cantuña and, on a corner, the Casa Gangotena. The plaza is built on ancient Incan ruins, including the palace of Emperor Atahualpa, which adds some history to the pictures you take. For a phone photographer there are two good angles. From the open plaza you can step back and frame the full church front with the square in the foreground. For a quieter and more varied picture, climb to the terrace in front of the church and look south. From there you see the dome of the Casa Gangotena in the foreground and the hill of El Panecillo behind it. Late afternoon is a good time to try, as one guide notes the sun sets over the church and the distant Pichincha volcano. Another guide prefers sunrise, so you could try both if you are staying nearby. Keep your phone upright for the facade and watch for people crossing the frame. A few figures on the square help show how big the church is.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Centre (Centro Histórico) of Quito, on the square in front of the Church and Convent of St. Francis, with the Casa Gangotena on one corner.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for the Historic Centre of Quito and ask for Plaza de San Francisco. That is roughly 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the terrace view toward El Panecillo. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the plaza to fit the whole church front. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out El Panecillo and the Casa Gangotena dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (the terrace in front of the church, looking south across the plaza). A view from the church front toward El Panecillo, with the dome of the Casa Gangotena hotel in the foreground. The plaza itself lies to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome and the hill on separate lines so they don't merge. For the wide alternative, walk east down into the plaza and frame the whitewashed church and monastery front with the open square in the foreground. Keep the phone level so the facade doesn't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the hill to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls and bright sky keep their detail. If you shoot toward the setting sun, try a Live Photo or take several frames at different exposures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is recommended, when the sun sets over the church and the distant Pichincha volcano. Guides do not agree on the best hour, and one favours sunrise.

text.access_note: The plaza and the terrace in front of the church are open to walk around, but the church interior, museum and bell towers charge an entrance fee, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps keep a tall facade from leaning.
Dropping the exposure slider slightly helps keep detail in white walls against a bright sky.
People in the frame give a sense of the scale of the church and square.
The plaza and terrace can be walked around without paying.
Take care in the Old Town after dark, as a reported mugging risk was flagged by one guide.

name: Casa del Alabado Museum of Pre-Columbian Art
label: Casa del Alabado
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/20231965: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Casa del Alabado Pre-Columbian Art Museum' (53 m across).
notes: Museum of pre-Columbian art in a colonial house.

text.description:
Casa del Alabado is a Pre-Columbian art museum in a colonial house built in the 17th century, during the Spanish colonial period. For a phone photographer it offers old-house character and ancient objects under one roof. The museum has two courtyards, eight exhibit rooms and a shop, so there are plenty of frames: the courtyards and individual objects.

About 500 of the 5,000-plus archaeological pieces in the collection are on permanent display. The rooms are organised by theme rather than by date, with subjects such as cosmology, ancestors, ritual and the natural world. The pieces are presented as works of art, which suits photography.

Start in a courtyard to capture the architecture of the house, then move inside for close shots of individual pieces. Keep your phone steady against your body or a wall and take a few frames of each subject, because indoor light can be low and some shots will come out soft. Look for strong shapes, such as a carved face or a curved vessel, and fill the frame with them. Keep other visitors out of the shot where you can, and be patient in the rooms. Rules on photography inside can vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Casa del Alabado is a Pre-Columbian art museum in Quito, Ecuador, housed in a 17th-century colonial house.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Use the phone icon on the map to find the museum building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyards to fit in the house and sky, and the default lens (1x) for rooms and display cases. Switch to 2x or more (telephoto) for details on objects when you can't get closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You photograph the house from its own courtyards and rooms rather than from a distant viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: In the courtyard, turn on gridlines and keep the walls and lines straight, then include a strip of sky. Inside, step close to one object at a time and let the plain background frame it. For a pleasing portrait of a piece, try portrait mode only if the edges of the object stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the object to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so lit pieces don't wash out. Turn the flash off. Hold the phone against your body or a wall to keep it steady in low light, and take a couple of frames of each piece.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go during opening hours, and for the courtyards choose a time of day when daylight is soft. Quieter moments make it easier to photograph objects without people in the frame.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so entry and photography rules apply: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Photography rules, including flash restrictions, may apply inside the museum.
Daylight in the courtyards is softer at some times of day than others.
Indoor light in the exhibit rooms can be low.
Some rooms may be busier at certain times, and quieter moments make it easier to photograph objects without people.

name: Itchimbía
label: Itchimbía Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque Itchimbía' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque Itchimbía' (way/327057802): edge nearest the subject (1151 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/89788: large area 'Itchimbia' (8478 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Hilltop park with a glass cultural centre and views of the old town.

text.description:
Itchimbía is a hill on the eastern edge of downtown Quito, with a park on top that is one of the easiest places to see the old centre spread out below you. The photo most visitors come for is the large 'Quito' lettering on the hilltop. With the letters in the foreground, the historic centre and the Basílica sit neatly behind them, so one frame says where you are. The top of the hill is also home to the Centro Cultural Itchimbía, a glass-walled building that holds an exhibition centre, a conference room and a museum. Its glass and iron frame make a good second picture, especially with the city showing through. Park entry is free.

Start on Parque Itchimbía near the letters. Keep the letters low in the frame and let the city fill the space behind them. If you have time, walk over to the glass building and shoot it from a few steps back so the whole structure fits. Early morning is also worth trying for a wider view across the city and towards the nearby volcanoes, with the hill's lookout in the frame. Paths are open and exposed, so a light layer is useful, as hilltops are often breezy.
text.geographic_location: Itchimbía is a hill on the eastern edge of downtown Quito, in Pichincha Province, with the La Alameda park just to its west. The park on top is the place to go for the 'Quito' letters and the glass cultural centre.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or other public transport stops are listed for this spot. Once at Parque Itchimbía, just east of the La Alameda park, head for the 'Quito' letters on the hilltop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the 'Quito' letters and the city behind them in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Basílica and the old centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque Itchimbía (near the 'Quito' letter sign on the hilltop). The Itchimbía hilltop in the foreground, with the large 'Quito' letters framing the historic centre and the Basílica behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the letters and the city share the frame. Crouch slightly so the letters stand out against the buildings. For a second picture, try the glass-walled Centro Cultural Itchimbía from a few steps back, with the city visible through the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the letters to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky looks washed out. In bright sun, wipe the lens first, as dust and fingerprints cause haze. Use panorama only if you can hold steady and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a good choice for a clear view across the city and the nearby volcanoes. Midday can look flat, so try to avoid it if you can.

text.access_note: Entry to the park is free, but check the official site before you go, especially for the Centro Cultural Itchimbía.

name: Church and convent of San Agustín, Quito
label: San Agustín Convent
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Guayaquil' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Calle Chile and Calle Guayaquil (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5117072: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Colonial convent where independence was declared in 1809.

text.description:
The Church and convent of San Agustín is a Catholic church run by the Augustinian Order, in the Historic Center of Quito. The Augustinians were given the site in 1573 and began the convent first. The church followed between 1606 and 1617, to plans drawn up by the architect Francisco Becerra. The main portal mixes Spanish and Amerindian decorative details, and the bell tower rises 37 metres, still holding its 17th-century bells. The convent's Chapter House is where the Act of the Governing Board of 1809 was signed, a moment linked to Quito's first cry of freedom.

From the street corner the church faces you head-on, so the portal and tower fit into one tall frame. That makes this an easy, rewarding stop for a phone. The street is fairly tight, so you will probably need to step back to the kerb or the opposite pavement to fit the tower in. If you want a wider, less head-on view, try the side street, Calle Mejía. Inside, there is a large painted ceiling and a palm-shaded colonial cloister, which suit quieter architectural shots. Inside the church, the main altar carries a huge 17th-century painting by Miguel de Santiago, "The Triumph of Saint Augustine". Keep the flash off inside, especially during a service, and check the official site before you go to find out which parts of the convent are open.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Center of Quito, on Calle Chile between Calle Guayaquil and Calle Flores. The church stands on the corner where Calle Chile meets Calle Guayaquil.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is given for this spot, so head for the Historic Center of Quito by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the corner of Calle Chile and Calle Guayaquil. Once you are in the Historic Center, you can also follow Calle Chile on foot, which leads straight to the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and tower from the pavement, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved portal and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Calle Chile and Calle Guayaquil (corner where the church sits, facing the facade). The church's Baroque facade and bell tower seen head-on from the street corner where the church stands.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the edges of the tower up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level, and hold it at chest height rather than tilting it up. If the tower will not fit, step back, or try Calle Mejía for a wider, angled view of the frontage on Calle Guayaquil. Inside, use the ultra-wide for the ceiling and cloister.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Inside, switch off the flash and use night mode for the dim church, resting your elbows on something solid to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is high enough to light the facade rather than leave it in shadow. Early in the day usually has fewer people on the pavement, but check the light on the day.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship, and the convent has its own entrance, so dress modestly and check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and which parts are open.

name: Centro Cultural Metropolitano
label: Centro Cultural Metro.
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31134646: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Centro Cultural Metropolitano' (162 m across).
notes: Cultural centre in a former Jesuit university building next to the main square.

text.description:
The Centro Cultural Metropolitano is in Quito, Ecuador, in a building that dates back to 1622. It has been a cultural institution since 1997, and before that it housed the First Central University and was also a jail where Spanish authorities executed insurgents during the Ecuadorian War of Independence. Although the building belongs to the colonial period, its facade was rebuilt in the 20th century, so what you see from the street is a mix of eras.

It photographs well because of its size and its plain, solid frontage. The outline of the complex is about 162 m across, which means a phone will struggle to take it all in from close range. Use the phone icon on the map as your starting position, then walk to the edge of the building, step back as far as the pavement allows and let the building fill the frame.

For a simple record shot, use the default lens (1x) with the gridlines switched on, so the facade lines stay straight. If you want more of the building and the street in one picture, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level or the walls will lean. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for details such as doorways, windows and carved stonework. Visitors may be able to go inside, but access can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Quito, Ecuador. The building dates from the colonial period.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot. Use the map to reach the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is too narrow to step back, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for doors, windows and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk to the edge of the building to find a clear view of the facade, and move along the pavement a little to find a good angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the facade with a vertical grid line so the walls stay straight. Keep the phone upright and level, and include a bit of street at the bottom for scale. Then take a second, closer shot of one doorway or window with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the street.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but entry to the building may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Basilica of La Merced, Quito
label: La Merced Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Merced' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Merced Plaza Perfumes Europeos' (node/4246911253): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/715095007: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Convento Máximo de La Merced' (102 m across).
notes: Baroque church with a tall bell tower.

text.description: The Basilica of La Merced is a white church in Quito's Historic Center. It was the first church and headquarters of the Mercedarian Order in Ecuador, which is why it has the title of basilica. It photographs well because the pale walls, square tower and five domes stand out against the busy old town around them. Look closely at the decoration too, which includes Inca and Arabic-style inscriptions. Building began in 1701, the tower was finished in 1736, and the church was consecrated in 1737. The convent next door also holds one of the city's most important historical libraries, though that is not part of the exterior view. The best phone picture comes from the open square in front, facing the façade, with plenty of space to fit the whole front and the tower into one frame. The square also gives you foreground interest, such as people crossing it towards the entrance. Calle Chile gives a different feel, with the white front as a backdrop to the old street and passers-by. Photography inside the church is generally not allowed, so plan on exterior shots only. Expect more people and festivities around the feast of the Virgin on 24 September, which can make for lively pictures but a crowded square.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Center of Quito, on the church's own corner at Calle Cuenca and Calle Chile, with Plaza de la Merced open in front of the façade.
text.directions_text: No Quito transport stop is given for this spot, so head for the Historic Center and walk to Plaza de la Merced. Once you are the church is to the north, about 1 minute on foot. Walk across the square towards the entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole façade, tower and square in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower and the decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la Merced (front of the church, from the open square facing the façade). The full white façade and ornate tower of the church, with the open square in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line so it does not lean. Keep a little of the square at the bottom of the frame to give a sense of scale. For a second view, walk to Calle Chile and frame the white front behind the old-town street and passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white walls to focus, then lower the exposure slider a touch so they keep their detail and do not wash out. If the sky is bright, check the tower's top edge on screen before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives gentler light on the white walls. Go early if you want fewer people in the square, and expect crowds around 24 September.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship, and photography inside is generally prohibited. Check locally for visiting arrangements.

name: Guápulo
label: Guápulo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mirador de Guápulo' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mirador de Guápulo' (node/380059957): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1557674: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Bohemian neighbourhood in a ravine with a colonial church.

text.description: Guápulo is a district of Quito that drops down a steep hillside, with a colonial church and its dome at the heart of the village. It is often described as Quito's artsy, bohemian corner, with local artists and a few laid-back cafés and bars. The Spaniards originally founded it as an independent city, and every year on 7 September the neighbourhood holds the Fiestas de Guápulo, with costumes, a parade, music and fireworks. The photo works best from above. From there you look down over the church and its dome, across the Cumbayá valley and the surrounding hills. On clear days you may also see volcanoes in the distance. Start with the default lens (1x) to get the church, the village roofs and the valley together in one frame. Then zoom in to 2x or 3x for a tighter picture of the dome. The village itself is a short walk downhill if you want street-level shots, but go in daylight and keep your phone close, as visitors mention safety concerns in the area. A second viewpoint is the church itself, where you can photograph the facade against the hillside. Ask staff before taking photos inside.
text.geographic_location: Guápulo is a district of Quito set behind Hotel Quito and below González Suárez. The Camino de Orellana winds down through it towards the road out to the neighbouring suburbs.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport listed for this spot, so start from the Hotel Quito and González Suárez area and head to the Mirador de Guápulo at Larrea and Pasaje Stübel. That is a rough straight-line distance, and the real route down may be steeper or longer. Confirm the mirador is open before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the church, village and valley together. Switch to 2x-3x (or up to 5x if your phone has it) to isolate the dome. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole valley, as the church will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mirador de Guápulo (Mirador at Larrea and Pasaje Stübel, hilltop above the village). Wide view over the Cumbayá valley and surrounding hills, with the Guápulo church and its dome visible below and volcanoes on clear days.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the church dome on one of the lower intersections, leaving the valley and hills to fill the rest of the frame. Keep the horizon level. If you have time, also photograph the church facade from the Santuario de Guápulo itself, as a second view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps some colour. For a wide sweep of the valley, try panorama mode and move slowly. In low light after sunset, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a steady surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives good light on the church, and sunrise or sunset are also recommended. Daylight is the sensible choice for safety.

text.access_note: The Mirador de Guápulo is a free public viewpoint, but it has been reported as closed, so check it is open before you go; interior photography rules at the church vary, so ask staff.
